edges.effect_quant: A meta-analysis of 9 randomized trials with 6853 participants found vitamin K2 increased lumbar-spine BMD change by 2.17% and forearm BMD by 1.57%, while a 48-week placebo-controlled trial in 63 women found significantly greater lumbar-BMD improvement and a 55.9% reduction in undercarboxylated osteocalcin with vitamin K2.
edges.population: postmenopausal women with osteoporosis or osteopenic bone loss
edges.mechanism: Vitamin K2 supports gamma-carboxylation of osteocalcin, helping bind calcium into bone matrix and lowering undercarboxylated osteocalcin. That gives a plausible route for modest support of bone mineralization, especially when combined with calcium and vitamin D.
edges.summary: Vitamin K2 shows a modest protective signal for postmenopausal bone health, especially on surrogate markers and small BMD gains, with the strongest enthusiasm coming from Japanese-style trials and meta-analytic pooling. It looks more like an adjunctive support therapy than a stand-alone replacement for established osteoporosis drugs.
edges.caveats: The literature is not perfectly consistent across formulations, background calcium/vitamin D use, and fracture endpoints. Benefits appear real but generally smaller and less definitive than those of first-line antiresorptive or anabolic osteoporosis therapies.
